text: Worcester Reed Warner (May 16, 1846 – June 25, 1929) was an American mechanical engineer, entrepreneur, manager, astronomer, and philanthropist. He co-founded the Warner & Swasey Company with Ambrose Swasey. The Moon's crater Warner is named after him. Born and raised on a farm near Cummington, Massachusetts, Warner met Swasey while both were apprentices at the Exeter Machine Works. In 1870, they both joined Pratt & Whitney in Hartford, Connecticut. In 1880, Warner and Swasey co-founded a business to manufacture sewing machines and lathes, but soon shifted to telescope manufacturing due to Warner’s interest in astronomy. The firm, initially located in Chicago, moved to Cleveland. In 1880, Beloit College purchased one of its telescopes, helping establish the company’s reputation in the telescope industry. Warner & Swasey designed and built the framework and mounting for the 36-inch refracting telescope installed at Lick Observatory in 1888, which was the world’s largest refractor at the time. The company later built telescopes used in Canada and Argentina. Warner was a charter member of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers and served as its 16th president from 1897 to 1898; Ambrose Swasey later became the 23rd president. In 1900, the firm was incorporated as the Warner & Swasey Company. Warner served as president and chairman of the board until his retirement in 1911. Both Warner and Swasey became trustees of the Case School of Applied Science and donated an entire observatory, which became the Warner and Swasey Observatory, dedicated in 1920. The Worcester Reed Warner Laboratory, located in the Warner Building at Case Western Reserve University, is named after Warner and was partly funded by him. In 1911, Warner and his family moved to Wilholm in the Wilson Park neighborhood of Tarrytown, New York, where he built a celestial observatory for stargazing sessions, inviting guests such as John D. Rockefeller and President Herbert Hoover. The Warner Library in Tarrytown, built and gifted by Warner and his wife Cornelia in 1929, is constructed of Vermont limestone and designed by Walter Dabney Blair. It cost $250,000 (approximately $4,700,000 in 2025 dollars) to build and was further endowed with $50,000 (about $950,000 in 2025 dollars) for books. Warner married Cornelia Blakemore of Philadelphia in 1890; they had three children, two of whom—Worcester Reed Warner Jr. and Marion Holbrook Warner—died at a young age. He was survived by daughter Helen Blakemore Warner (1894–1971), who used her inheritance to continue his philanthropy. She collaborated with John D. Rockefeller Jr. in saving and restoring the Philipsburg Manor House in Sleepy Hollow and established the Helen B. Warner Prize for Astronomy, awarded annually by the American Astronomical Society. In memory of her father’s birthplace, Cummington, Massachusetts, she founded the Cummington Museum, now known as the Kingman Tavern Historical Museum. She also supported the Cleveland Museum of Art and the Phelps Hospital. Warner died on a trip in Eisenach, Saxe-Weimar, Germany, four months after the dedication of the Warner Library, and is buried in Sleepy Hollow Cemetery. The Worcester Reed Warner Medal, established by his bequest in 1930, is awarded by the ASME for "outstanding contribution to the permanent literature of engineering."
